evidence.quote: Dead Horse Mesa Scenic Byway 22.5 miles | 30 minutes UT-313 is a 22.5 mile long scenic byway

evidence.claim: A county road already reached Dead Horse Point by 1969.
evidence.quote: The route that SR-313 runs along was mapped by 1969, stretching all the way to Dead Horse Point as an unmarked county highway.

evidence.claim: Utah took over maintenance and assigned SR-313 in 1975, replacing a proposed state route that was never built.
evidence.quote: In 1975, the proposal for SR-278 was cancelled. In its place, the Utah Department of Transportation assigned SR-313, assuming maintenance for what was local roads.

evidence.claim: After crews rebuilding the Canyonlands access road damaged SR-313, reconstruction began in 1989.
evidence.quote: The access road to Canyonlands National Park was rebuilt 1988, and the construction crews severely damaged SR-313 in the process. The highway was completely rebuilt, starting in 1989, to its modern form.

evidence.claim: The work reduced the maximum grade from 11 percent to 8 percent and leveled the switchbacks to remove blind corners.
evidence.quote: The reconstruction reduced the maximum grade from 11% to 8% and re-graded the switchbacks to be on level ground to eliminate the blind corners.

evidence.claim: a proposed state route that was never built.
evidence.quote: SR-278 was never constructed.

evidence.claim: Begin at US-191, about nine miles north of Moab, and climb toward the plateau.
evidence.quote: After about 9 miles (14.5 km), look for the “Dead Horse Point State Park” sign and turn left (west) onto SR-313. This is the start of the byway.

evidence.claim: At about 14.6 miles, the left fork leads to Dead Horse Point.
evidence.quote: At about 14.6 miles (23.5km) from the beginning of SR-313 a fork to the left leads to Dead Horse Point State Park.

evidence.claim: Return to SR-313, then continue toward Canyonlands’ Island in the Sky district and Grand View Point.
evidence.quote: After leaving Dead Horse Point State Park, backtrack to Highway 313, turn left, and head toward the Island in the Sky District of Canyonlands National Park, ultimately ending at Grandview Point.

evidence.claim: Two Civil War ship names turn up above Sevenmile Canyon: Monitor and Merrimac.
evidence.quote: The two buttes were named after the Monitor and Merrimack, two ironclad steamships known for clashing during the American Civil War.

evidence.quote: They can be seen from Highway 313 after it climbs out of Sevenmile Canyon

evidence.quote: Dead Horse Point State Park features an 8-mile (13 km) hiking trail that includes loops and overlooks on the East Rim Trail and the West Rim Trail.

evidence.claim: Stone granaries near the top of Aztec Butte held food gathered by Ancestral Puebloan people who traveled to Island in the Sky to hunt and collect seeds.

evidence.claim: The granaries date to AD 1200–1300.
evidence.quote: These well-preserved granaries date to AD 1200–1300.

evidence.claim: The butte itself is white, cross-bedded Navajo Sandstone, the remains of wind-borne dunes deposited approximately 170 million years ago.

evidence.claim: From the Upheaval Dome road, a half-mile trail across flat grassland leads to a quarter-mile scramble gaining 200 feet to the top and granaries.
evidence.quote: A half-mile hiking trail through flat grassland, followed by a quarter-mile scramble with 200 feet vertical gain, leads to the top of the butte and the granaries. The trailhead is located alongside the road to Upheaval Dome.

flags: Route scope differs: Utah tourism describes the 22.5-mile SR-313; Moab tourism describes a longer drive including the Island in the Sky road to Grand View Point. Mileage and time are kept with their respective scopes. No cached evidence supports the catalog’s exact designation date.
The SR-313 page contradicts itself on toll direction. The practical note follows Moab tourism’s statement that a fee is required to proceed to the viewpoints; no fee amount is supplied.
Aztec Butte’s trail and granaries are described only by a cached encyclopedia page; current trail conditions and access have not been verified by a park-manager source.

The cached naming legend for Dead Horse Point lacks a named originator. It is omitted in favor of observable landscape and plant adaptations; the current draft’s Aztec Butte date hedge was removed because the source gives AD 1200–1300 without a hedge.
